_note: Scrollbook-only overrides, keyed by slug. Any field here replaces the episode's value on /scrollbook pages only; the Acquired pages keep episodes.json. `articles` is the daily reading plan: one article a day; `at` (seconds) is where its audio starts, otherwise the audio is split evenly. `demoRead` shows that many articles as already read until the visitor has progress of their own (demo only).

articles.title: A kingdom adrift
articles.dek: By 1984 the company Walt built was earning more from real estate than from movies, and raiders were circling.

articles.title: The raid
articles.dek: Saul Steinberg's greenmail bid, and how a near-hostile takeover forced the family to look outside for leaders.

articles.title: Eisner and Wells
articles.dek: A Paramount hitmaker and a Warner Bros. operator, hired as a pair. Why the split of roles mattered.

articles.title: Mining the vault
articles.dek: Home video turned old classics into a cash machine almost overnight, and paid for everything that came next.

articles.title: The parks reprice
articles.dek: Ticket prices had barely moved in years. Raising them was the fastest profit lever the new team had.

articles.title: The Little Mermaid
articles.dek: Howard Ashman, Alan Menken and the Broadway formula that brought feature animation back from the edge.

articles.title: The Renaissance run
articles.dek: Beauty and the Beast, Aladdin, The Lion King: five years that rebuilt the brand and the merchandise business.

articles.title: A deal with Pixar
articles.dek: A small computer-animation studio in Richmond, a three-picture contract, and Toy Story.

articles.title: Buying ABC
articles.dek: Capital Cities/ABC for $19 billion, and with it ESPN, the most valuable asset Disney would own for decades.

articles.title: The long decline
articles.dek: Wells' death, the Ovitz fiasco and a falling-out with Pixar. How the second Eisner decade went wrong.

articles.title: Save Disney
articles.dek: Roy E. Disney's campaign, the 43% no-vote, and the board's choice of a quiet operator named Bob Iger.

articles.title: Iger buys Pixar
articles.dek: His first big move: pay $7.4 billion for the studio Disney had fallen out with, and hand it the keys to animation.

articles.title: Marvel and Lucasfilm
articles.dek: Two more franchise libraries bought within three years, each one built into a decade of films and parks.

articles.title: The empire, assembled
articles.dek: Fox, Disney+ and the flywheel at full size. What the comeback teaches about owning stories people return to.
